lesson_title: Double the Sides, Quadruple the Carpet
hook_text: Double every side of a shape and the fence around it doubles. The carpet inside does not double. Guess how much it grows.
clip_script: Here is a 6 by 4 rectangle. Fence around it: 20. Carpet inside it: 24. Now double every side: 12 by 8. Fence: 12 plus 8 plus 12 plus 8, which is 40. Exactly double. Carpet: 12 times 8, which is 96. Not double. Four times. Why? Draw the big one and cut it with one line across and one line down. Four copies of the small one, two across and two down. Four carpets, but every fence side is just twice as long. Length is one-dimensional, so doubling hits it once. Area is two-dimensional, so doubling hits it twice: two times two is four. Triple the sides and the carpet is nine times. Any scale factor k: fence times k, carpet times k squared. That is why a 30 centimetre pizza is four 15 centimetre pizzas, and why doubling a photo's size costs four times the paper. Say it: fence doubles, carpet quadruples.
visual_style: A 6 by 4 rectangle on a whiteboard grows into a 12 by 8 one; a horizontal and vertical line split it into four glowing copies of the original; the fence traces around the outside twice as long; k and k squared appear as a two-line rule; a pizza splits into four.
pacing: Numbers fast, the four-copies picture slow, the one-dimension versus two-dimensions idea at speaking pace, the k rule and the pizza as a quick close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for doubling one dimension only, circles, the backwards square root and the map scale trap.
